title: Linkers, Libraries and Loading
oneLiner: How separately compiled files become one program, what "undefined reference" really means, and static vs dynamic libraries.
keyTakeaway: A compiler turns each source file into an object file that defines some symbols and refers to others it can't see. The linker combines the object files and libraries, matches every reference to exactly one definition, lays the code out in memory, and patches each call with its final address. No definition gives an "undefined reference" error; two definitions give "multiple definition". Static libraries are copied into the executable at link time; shared libraries (.so, .dll) are found and bound when the program loads.
explanation:
C and C++ compile one source file at a time. Compiling main.c produces main.o, an object file with machine code, data, and a symbol table: the names this file defines (main) and the names it uses but doesn't define (parse_args, printf). At every place the code uses an undefined name, the compiler leaves a placeholder address and a relocation entry that says "put the address of parse_args here". The compiler never sees the other files, which is why a declaration in a header (a file of declarations shared between source files) is enough to compile a call but not to run it.

The linker (ld, lld or MSVC's link.exe) does four things. It reads all the object files and libraries. It resolves symbols, matching each undefined reference to exactly one definition. It merges the sections (all code together, all data together) and assigns every function and global a final address. Then it applies the relocations, patching each placeholder with the real address, and writes an executable. If a reference has no definition you get "undefined reference to parse_args" (LNK2019 on Windows). If two object files both define the same non-static symbol, you get "multiple definition" (LNK2005). Marking a C function static, or putting it in an anonymous namespace in C++, makes it local to its file so it never clashes.

A static library (libfoo.a, foo.lib) is an archive of object files. The linker copies in only the members that resolve a symbol something still needs, and the code becomes part of your executable: one self-contained file, but every program carries its own copy and must be relinked to pick up a fix. GNU ld also scans archives in command-line order, so a library listed before the files that use it can still produce undefined references. A shared library (libc.so.6, kernel32.dll) is linked dynamically: the linker records only that the program needs it, and the dynamic linker loads it and binds the symbols when the program starts, often lazily on first call through a procedure linkage table. One copy in memory is shared by every process, and a security fix to the library fixes every program, but the program fails at startup if the library is missing or incompatible.

Managed languages move most of this to run time. A C# project references other assemblies by name and version; the CLR finds, loads and binds them when a method first needs them, so a missing assembly shows up as a FileNotFoundException at run time, not a link error. Native AOT brings a real link step back, and the IL trimmer removes unused code first. Python resolves import statements when they execute, which is why a typo in an import inside a rarely called function only fails when that function runs. For what happens when the program is started and the dynamic linker runs, see What Happens When You Run a Program.
